paragraphs.title: Jehoshaphat’s Return and the Prophetic Rebuke

easy.explanation: Jehoshaphat returned in peace to his house in Jerusalem.
easy.q: Where did Jehoshaphat return after the war?

easy.explanation: Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet and rebuke Jehoshaphat.
The passage says that Jehoshaphat took away the groves from the land.
easy.q: Which good deed of Jehoshaphat is mentioned?

answers: Because he did not return to Jerusalem
Because he helped the ungodly and loved those who hated the LORD
medium.explanation: Jehu rebuked Jehoshaphat for helping the ungodly and loving those who hated the LORD.
medium.q: Why was the LORD angry with Jehoshaphat?

answers: He mentions both Jehoshaphat’s fault and his good deeds
medium.explanation: The passage criticizes one action while also acknowledging good things found in Jehoshaphat.
medium.q: How does the prophet combine criticism with recognition of Jehoshaphat’s good actions?

medium.explanation: Wrath refers to the LORD’s anger because of Jehoshaphat’s actions.
medium.q: What does the word “wrath” mean in this passage?

answers: That he had no faults at all
That the rebuke concerned a particular action and did not erase his good deeds
That the prophet praised his help to the ungodly
challenge.explanation: The passage presents criticism of one action together with recognition of Jehoshaphat’s good deeds.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from Jehoshaphat’s returning in peace even though he was rebuked?

answers: Jehoshaphat prepared himself inwardly to seek and serve God
Jehoshaphat prepared an army for war
challenge.explanation: The phrase describes an inward determination to seek God.
challenge.q: What is meant by “thou hast ... prepared thine heart to seek God”?

answers: Both describe turning away from idolatry and drawing near to God
There is no connection in the passage
challenge.explanation: Removing the groves and seeking God are both presented as faithful actions.
challenge.q: What connection exists between taking away the groves and preparing the heart to seek God?

paragraphs.title: Restoring the People to God and Appointing Judges

easy.explanation: Jehoshaphat went through the people from Beersheba to mount Ephraim.
easy.q: From what place to what place did Jehoshaphat travel among the people?

answers: To the LORD God of their fathers
easy.explanation: The passage says that he brought the people back unto the LORD God of their fathers.
easy.q: To whom did Jehoshaphat bring the people back?

easy.explanation: Jehoshaphat set judges throughout all the fenced cities of Judah.
easy.q: What did Jehoshaphat set in the fenced cities of Judah?

answers: He brought the people back to the LORD and then appointed judges
He stopped attending to the people
medium.explanation: After the prophet’s message, Jehoshaphat pursued spiritual restoration and orderly judgment.
medium.q: What did Jehoshaphat do after Jehu’s message?

answers: To judge the people and maintain order in each city
medium.explanation: The judges were appointed to administer justice throughout the cities.
medium.q: Why were judges appointed in Judah’s cities?

medium.explanation: Fenced cities were cities protected by fortifications.
medium.q: What does “fenced” mean in the phrase “the fenced cities of Judah”?

answers: He acted only inside his palace
He personally worked to restore the people and improve the nation
challenge.explanation: The passage describes Jehoshaphat going among the people and acting throughout the land.
challenge.q: What does Jehoshaphat’s traveling throughout the land reveal about his leadership?

answers: Appointing judges, then restoring the people
Restoring the people to the LORD, then appointing judges
Going to war, then appointing judges
challenge.explanation: Jehoshaphat first brought the people back to the LORD and then set judges in the cities.
challenge.q: Which sequence of actions is described in these verses?

answers: Both were steps toward spiritual and social restoration
challenge.explanation: Jehoshaphat strengthened both the people’s worship and the nation’s system of justice.
challenge.q: What connection exists between bringing the people back to the LORD and appointing judges?

easy.explanation: Jehoshaphat told them that they judged not merely for man, but for the LORD.
easy.q: Before whom did the judges judge, according to Jehoshaphat?

easy.explanation: He commanded that the fear of the LORD should be upon them.
easy.q: What did Jehoshaphat command the judges to have upon them?

answers: Iniquity, respect of persons, and taking of gifts
easy.explanation: The passage forbids iniquity, respect of persons, and taking gifts.
easy.q: Which forbidden actions are mentioned in these verses?

answers: It should lead them to act with reverence and responsibility
It should allow them to favor their friends
It should release them from judging
medium.explanation: Serving before the LORD required the judges to act carefully and justly.
medium.q: How should knowing that they judged before the LORD affect the judges?

answers: Showing favoritism because of a person’s status or identity
medium.explanation: Respect of persons means showing unfair preference to someone.
medium.q: What does “respect of persons” mean in this context?

answers: To warn against distorting judgment in different ways
To teach the judges how to receive presents
medium.explanation: Both bribery and favoritism can corrupt a just decision.
medium.q: Why does Jehoshaphat mention both gifts and respect of persons?

answers: They judge human beings, but must remember that they act before the LORD
They should not judge people at all
They may judge only matters of war
challenge.explanation: The instruction joins their human duty as judges with their accountability before the LORD.
challenge.q: What is the central contrast in Jehoshaphat’s instruction to the judges?

answers: Both carefulness and practical action are required
Good intentions without action are enough
The judges should avoid making decisions
challenge.explanation: The command requires the judges both to be careful and to carry out their duty.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the command, “take heed and do it”?

answers: All of them harm fair judgment
All of them concern the groves
All of them protect the weak
challenge.explanation: Each practice is opposed to honesty and righteous judgment.
challenge.q: What principle is shared by iniquity, respect of persons, and taking gifts?

easy.explanation: Jehoshaphat set the court in Jerusalem.
easy.q: Where did Jehoshaphat establish the central court?

easy.explanation: The court included Levites, priests, and the chief of the fathers of Israel.
easy.q: Who were included among the members of the court?

answers: The judgment of the LORD and controversies
easy.explanation: They were appointed for the judgment of the LORD and for controversies.
easy.q: What matters did the court handle?

answers: To warn them so that they would not trespass against the LORD
To recruit them for the army
medium.explanation: The court was to warn the people so that they would not incur guilt before the LORD.
medium.q: What responsibility did the court have toward the people?

answers: Blood, law, commandment, statutes, and judgments
medium.explanation: The passage lists matters between blood and blood, law and commandment, statutes and judgments.
medium.q: Which kinds of matters were included among the controversies brought before them?

medium.explanation: A controversy is a dispute brought before the court for judgment.
medium.q: What does “controversies” mean in this context?

answers: So it could handle both the LORD’s law and the people’s disputes
So it could replace the king
So it could command the army
challenge.explanation: The court’s membership suited its religious, public, and community responsibilities.
challenge.q: Why was the court composed of religious leaders and chief fathers?

answers: The warning was meant to keep the people from trespassing and bringing wrath
The warning was meant to punish the whole people
There is no connection between them
challenge.explanation: The passage says that failure to warn could result in wrath upon the leaders and the people.
challenge.q: What is the connection between warning the people and preventing wrath from coming upon the community?

answers: It dealt with a wide range of binding matters
It dealt only with family disputes
challenge.explanation: The detailed list emphasizes the broad scope of the court’s responsibility.
challenge.q: What does the list “law and commandment, statutes and judgments” show about the court?

paragraphs.title: The Division of Responsibility and Encouragement to Leaders

easy.explanation: Amariah was over the people in all matters of the LORD.
easy.q: Over what matters was Amariah the chief priest placed?

easy.explanation: Zebadiah was the ruler of Judah for all the king’s matters.
easy.q: Over what matters was Zebadiah the son of Ishmael placed?

easy.explanation: The passage says that the Levites would be officers before the leaders.
easy.q: What role did the Levites have?

answers: Amariah handled matters of the LORD, and Zebadiah handled the king’s matters
Amariah handled the king’s matters, and Zebadiah handled matters of the LORD
Both were responsible only for the army
medium.explanation: The verse distinguishes between the LORD’s matters and the king’s matters.
medium.q: How was responsibility divided between Amariah and Zebadiah?

medium.explanation: The encouragement was given to those serving in positions of leadership.
medium.q: To whom was the command, “Deal courageously,” directed?

answers: The LORD will be with those who do what is good
The LORD will abolish all laws
The LORD will appoint a new king
medium.explanation: The phrase encourages faithful action with confidence in the LORD’s support.
medium.q: What does “the LORD shall be with the good” mean?

answers: There was a distinction between religious and royal responsibility
Only the priests were responsible for everything
challenge.explanation: The verse defines different areas of responsibility within Judah’s leadership.
challenge.q: What does the division of duties between Amariah and Zebadiah show?

answers: The judges decided cases, while the officers helped maintain order and carry out decisions
The Levites replaced the priests in worship
The Levites dealt only with war
challenge.explanation: Officers provided practical support for the work of the leaders and judges.
challenge.q: How did the Levites’ role as officers complement the role of the judges?

answers: The promise encouraged the leaders to act boldly and righteously
The promise excused them from responsibility
The promise removed the division of duties
challenge.explanation: The encouragement joins responsible action with confidence in the LORD’s presence.
challenge.q: What is the connection between the command to be courageous and the promise that the LORD is with the good?
